passage: Ankita, you froze when the director praised your report, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Francis. At twenty-five I finished a bridge inspection ahead of schedule, and the chief engineer thanked me in front of everyone. My face went hot and I wanted the attention gone, so I said, "Oh, it was nothing, anyone could do it." The chief looked disappointed, and a colleague told me later it felt like I had thrown his thanks back. Years on, when praise came again, I said, "Thank you, sir. It helped that Sajan covered the night readings." Just that. The chief nodded, Sajan grinned, and nobody had to pretend anything. Thank first, then hand out whatever credit is due.

qa.q: What did Francis say when the chief engineer thanked Francis at twenty-five?
qa.a: Francis said, "Oh, it was nothing, anyone could do it."

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when brushing off the thanks?
qa.a: Francis's face went hot and Francis wanted the attention gone, so Francis was probably embarrassed. Modesty is another possible reading.

qa.q: What did Francis change the second time praise came?
qa.a: Francis said thank you first and then gave credit to Sajan for covering the night readings.

qa.q: How did the chief engineer seem to take the first reply?
qa.a: The chief looked disappointed, and Francis was told later that it felt as if the chief's thanks had been thrown back.

grounding: A young adult who once deflected thanks learns to accept recognition with a simple thank-you and credit to others.

passage: The canteen was so loud that Mahima had to lean in to be heard. The maintenance team's shift change was five minutes away, and Deepak was still holding his tray. "The generator fix on Saturday saved our whole batch," Mahima said. "Thank you. Truly." Deepak's first instinct was to laugh it off. Instead he put the tray down and said, "Thank you, that means a lot. Naveen did the wiring, and I handled the testing." Mahima smiled, noted both names for the weekly update, and hurried off. Deepak stood there a second with warm ears, then went to find Naveen to tell him.

qa.q: How soon was the maintenance team's shift change?
qa.a: It was five minutes away.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling as he stood there with warm ears?
qa.a: He felt pleased 😊 and a little shy at being thanked, and he wanted Naveen to hear it too. Warm ears could also just be the heat of the canteen.

qa.q: What made Deepak's reply a good way to accept thanks?
qa.a: He said thank you plainly and named Naveen's wiring, so he neither waved it off nor kept all the credit.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt if Deepak had laughed it off?
qa.a: Mahima might have felt unheard, as if Mahima's thanks did not count, and been less likely to speak up next time.

grounding: A young adult accepts thanks with a warm acknowledgement and credits another person instead of deflecting or boasting, under time pressure in a noisy place.

passage: At the Sunday meeting of the Velachery residents' association, Hemant, the secretary, stood up with a printout. "Before anything else: Varun organised the lake-edge clean-up last week. Sixty volunteers, forty bags of rubbish, and he got the corporation truck to come on a Sunday. Thank you, Varun." People clapped. Varun's ears went red. "Arre, it was nothing, anyone could have done it," he said, waving a hand. Hemant's smile flickered; he lowered the printout a little, as if he'd said something wrong. Varun saw it. He'd done this all his life, batting praise away, and he suddenly realised it made the other person feel foolish for offering it. He stood up. "Actually, thank you, Hemant. I'm proud of it. And the real credit goes to the Class 9 kids from the school, who worked four hours straight." The kids at the back cheered. Hemant grinned and sat down.

qa.q: How many bags of rubbish were collected?
qa.a: Forty bags of rubbish.

qa.q: How did Hemant seem to feel when Varun said 'it was nothing'?
qa.a: Hemant seemed deflated and a little foolish, his smile flickering and the printout lowering, as if his thanks had been a mistake.

qa.q: How did Varun receive the praise the second time?
qa.a: He thanked Hemant simply, admitted being proud, and credited the Class 9 kids, balancing acceptance with credit to others.

qa.q: How might the Class 9 kids have felt when Varun credited them?
qa.a: They were delighted and proud, cheering from the back at being publicly recognised for four hours of work.

grounding: Shows a young adult brushing off public thanks, noticing it leaves the giver unheard, and then accepting warmly while crediting others.

passage:
"Farida, can I say something? Thank you for covering the client call on Friday. You saved me."
Farida didn't look up from her screen. "Oh, please. It was nothing. Anyone would have done it."
"It wasn't nothing. You stayed till eight."
"I had to stay anyway. Honestly, don't mention it."
Devika stood there a moment. "Okay," she said quietly, and turned to go.
Farida heard the flatness in it and looked up. "Wait. Sorry. I do that. My mother taught us to wave compliments away." She took a breath. "Thank you for saying it. I'm glad it helped, and I'm glad you noticed."
Devika's face relaxed. "I did. The client emailed to say the call was the clearest they'd had."
"Really?" Farida smiled. "Then Raghav deserves some of that. He built the slides."
"I'll tell him too."
"Tell him first."

qa.q: Until what time did Farida stay on Friday?
qa.a: Till eight.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Farida kept brushing off the thanks?
qa.a: Devika felt unheard and a bit hurt, her 'Okay' going flat as she turned to leave.

qa.q: What did Farida do to receive the thanks well?
qa.a: She apologised for brushing it off, thanked Devika, said she was glad it helped, and credited Raghav for the slides.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when he hears about the client's email?
qa.a: Raghav would likely feel pleased and valued, since his slides were credited for the clearest call the client had had.

grounding: Shows a young professional deflecting thanks until she notices the giver feels unheard, then accepting warmly and crediting a colleague.

passage: When I won the young achiever award at our NGO last year, I gave a speech I still cringe at. I talked for four minutes about the literacy project: my idea, my late nights, my plan. I didn't mention Amandeep once, and she had run every single Saturday session at the settlement school with me. I saw her clapping politely at the back, not quite smiling. Afterwards she said lightly, "Nice speech, Alka," and went home early. It took me two days to understand. I had swung from the modest girl who used to say "it was nothing" to someone who took all the credit. So I called her. "I left you out. That was wrong. The project is half yours." She was quiet, then said, "Thank you for saying that." This year, when our director thanked me in the staff meeting, I said, "Thank you. I'm proud of it. Amandeep and I built it together." She squeezed my arm.

qa.q: What did Amandeep run with Alka?
qa.a: Every Saturday session at the settlement school.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt during Alka's award speech?
qa.a: Amandeep likely felt hurt and overlooked, clapping politely without really smiling and going home early.

qa.q: How did Alka balance recognition the second time?
qa.a: She said a simple thank-you, admitted pride, and credited Amandeep as co-builder, neither deflecting nor taking all the credit.

qa.q: What would have changed if Alka had never called Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep's hurt might have hardened into distrust, and their partnership on the project could have weakened.

grounding: A young adult recalls taking all the credit in an award speech, repairing it, and later accepting thanks warmly while crediting a partner.

passage:
Coach's note, Sunday, after the district relay
Aditi ran the anchor leg today and pulled us from third to first. At the finish, Arohi, who had run the opening leg, hugged her and said, "You were unbelievable!" Aditi shook her head. "No, no, I was slow off the handover. It was luck." Arohi's smile faded, and she walked off to her bag.
I've seen this before with Aditi. Every compliment bounces off.
At the cool-down I told her, quietly, that when she brushes praise away, the person giving it can feel they've been told they're wrong. I suggested trying just "thank you," and naming anyone who helped.
At the team dinner, the club secretary raised a glass to her. Aditi went pink, paused, and said, "Thank you. And Arohi's start gave me the lead to work with." Arohi grinned across the table.
Something to keep practising next season.

qa.q: Which leg did Aditi run?
qa.a: Aditi ran the anchor leg.

qa.q: What might Aditi's going pink and pausing at dinner suggest?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt shy and a little awkward receiving praise but chose to accept it; the flush could also be simple pleasure.

qa.q: What did the coach suggest Aditi try?
qa.a: Saying just "thank you" and naming anyone who helped, instead of brushing the praise away.

qa.q: How did Arohi experience the two responses?
qa.a: At the finish Arohi felt brushed off and walked away to her bag; at dinner, when credited for her start, she grinned.

grounding: A young adult who deflects every compliment leaves the giver feeling unheard, and a warm thank-you with credit to others balances it.
